name: Szczerbiec
powers: Symbol of Polish kingship; the notched blade carries the Kiev legend.
description: Szczerbiec, the jagged sword used at Polish coronations from the Middle Ages. Its name, 'the notched one', recalls the legend that Bolesław the Brave struck it against the Golden Gate of Kiev in 1018. The surviving blade, now in Wawel Castle, was damaged in a nineteenth-century theft.
source: Wawel Crown Jewels; coronation tradition

name: Crown of Saint Wenceslas
material: Gold set with rubies, sapphires and emeralds
description: The Crown of Saint Wenceslas, made in 1347 for Charles IV and used to crown Bohemian kings. It is set with rubies, sapphires and emeralds and kept with the other Czech crown jewels. Legend holds that any usurper who sets it on his head will die within a year; it is shown only rarely and under strict conditions.
source: Bohemian crown jewels; Prague legend

name: Lajkonik
description: The Lajkonik is a hobby-horse rider of Kraków, a masked figure dressed as a Tatar warrior who parades the Old Town on the octave of Corpus Christi, striking onlookers with a wooden mace for luck. The procession commemorates the defeat of a Mongol raid, and the figure has been a beloved Kraków festival emblem for centuries.
source: Ethnographic studies of Kraków folk festivals

name: Rogatywka
description: The rogatywka is a four-pointed peaked cap of Polish tradition, evolved from the konfederatka worn by Bar Confederation troops in 1768 and later the standard Polish military cap. Its four corners mark the four sides of the world, and it remains a national and military symbol worn in parades and folk ensembles.
source: Histories of Polish military dress

name: Wycinanka
description: Wycinanka is Polish folk paper-cutting, most famously the colourful layered cutouts of Łowicz, made with sheep shears from dyed paper. Designs show birds, suns, flowers and village scenes, and were pasted on walls and beams to brighten rural homes, particularly in Mazovia and Kurpie regions.
source: Studies of Polish folk paper-cutting

name: Kraków Szopka
description: The Kraków szopka is a colourful Nativity crib built as a miniature of Kraków's architecture, with towers, spires and gilt foil, crafted by krakowianie and judged each December in a contest at the Rynek. The tradition, inscribed by UNESCO in 2018, blends the Nativity scene with civic pride and Christmas carolling.
source: UNESCO intangible heritage files and Kraków ethnography

name: Pomlázka
description: The pomlázka is a braided whip of willow twigs used on Easter Monday in the Czech lands, when boys lightly switch girls to keep them fresh and healthy, receiving painted eggs in return. Made of eight to twelve woven twigs bound with ribbon, it carries an old spring-renewal meaning in Czech folk custom.
source: Czech and Slovak ethnography of Easter customs

name: Czech Glass Christmas Ornaments
description: Czech glass Christmas ornaments are hand-blown and hand-painted glass baubles produced around Jablonec nad Nisou since the mid-19th century. Tiny beads and figurines are strung for the tree, and the region's skilled glassworkers made Christmas ornaments a famous export prized for their delicate silvering and colours.
source: Histories of Bohemian glassmaking

name: Fujara
description: The fujara is a long overtone flute of Slovak shepherds, up to two metres long, made from elder or maple wood with a unique air duct. Played while standing, it produces a deep humming bass; its sound and technique were inscribed by UNESCO in 2008 as a living shepherd tradition.
source: UNESCO intangible heritage files and Slovak ethnomusicology

name: Drotárstvo (Wire Craft)
description: Drotárstvo, or wire craft, is the Slovak art of reinforcing cracked pottery and glass with fine iron wire, practised by travelling drotár craftsmen from the 18th century. Wire-bound jugs, bottles and bowls became folk masterpieces, and the craft was inscribed on UNESCO's intangible heritage list in 2019.
source: UNESCO intangible heritage files and Slovak ethnography

name: Valaška
description: The valaška is the small shepherd's axe of the Carpathian Highlands, a light axe on a long decorated wooden handle used as a staff, tool and weapon by Slovak bača shepherds. Legend credits it as the weapon of Jánošík, and it became a badge of the highland shepherd's life.
material: forged iron blade, carved wood handle
source: Slovak folklore and highland ethnography

name: Martenitsa
description: The martenitsa is a Bulgarian talisman of twisted red and white yarn, with a small pendant, given on 1 March to wish health and spring. Worn on the wrist until a stork or blossom appears, it honours Baba Marta, and the shared custom is inscribed on UNESCO's intangible heritage list.
source: Bulgarian ethnography of spring customs and UNESCO files

name: Kukeri
description: The kukeri are Bulgarian winter ritual figures, men dressed in sheepskin costumes with tall carved wooden masks, animal hides and heavy bronze bells who dance through villages at New Year and before Lent to drive away evil spirits and bring fertility. The rite is strongest in the Pernik and Shoppe regions.
material: sheepskin, carved wood, goat hair, bronze bells
source: Bulgarian ethnography of winter ritual customs

name: Gaida
description: The gaida is the Bulgarian bagpipe, a goatskin bag with a chanter and drone, played at weddings, festivals and shepherds' pastures. Its bright, reedy voice leads horo dances, and it is considered the most beloved national instrument of Bulgarian folk music.
source: Bulgarian ethnomusicology

name: Šajkača
description: The šajkača is the Serbian cap with a raised V-shaped crown, descended from the cloth caps of the 18th-century šajkaši river troops who patrolled the Danube. Worn by Serbian soldiers and peasants, and in the Serbian military tradition, it became a national headgear symbol.
source: Histories of Serbian military dress and ethnography

name: Pirot Kilim
description: The Pirot kilim is a handwoven wool rug of the town of Pirot in southern Serbia, made on a vertical loom with geometric medallions and borders in red, black, green and white. Woven for centuries for floors, walls and weddings, it is counted a national symbol of Serbian weaving.
source: Serbian textile and craft studies

name: Opanak
description: The opanak is traditional Serbian peasant footwear, a soft leather moccasin with a turned-up pointed toe and leather straps, hand-made and waterproof. Its curling toe, worn for walking in grass and hills, made it a marker of Serbian village identity and folk dress.
source: Serbian folk dress studies

name: Ohrid Pearl
description: Ohrid pearls are handmade jewellery pearls of North Macedonia, formed by layering fish-scale essence over a mother-of-pearl core, made in Ohrid workshops for about a century. Their warm lustre and entirely manual method made them a signature craft of Ohrid and the region's jewellers.
source: Macedonian craft and jewellery studies

name: Dvojanka
description: The dvojanka is a North Macedonian double flute, two parallel pipes carved from one piece of wood or bone with fingerholes on one pipe, played by shepherds. Its paired pipes sound a drone with the melody, and it accompanies Macedonian pastoral and festive music.
source: Macedonian ethnomusicology

name: Koschei's Needle
description: Needle in which the Russian fairy-tale villain Koschei the Deathless hides his soul, so that he cannot be killed while it remains intact. In Afanasyev's collected tales the needle lies inside an egg, the egg inside a duck, the duck inside a hare, and the hare inside a chest on an island oak; the hero must break the needle to destroy Koschei. The motif recurs across Slavic and wider folklore.
material: iron needle (in the tale, nested in egg, duck, hare, chest)
source: Afanasyev, 'Russian Fairy Tales' (Koschei the Deathless)

name: Baba Yaga's Mortar and Pestle
description: Iron mortar and pestle ridden by Baba Yaga, the witch of Russian fairy tales, who flies over the forest in her mortar, sweeping away her trail with a broom and driving the mortar onward with the pestle. In Afanasyev's tales she is called 'Baba Yaga the Bone Leg' and travels in this way; the mortar, pestle and broom are among the most iconic props of Russian folk narrative.
source: Afanasyev, 'Russian Fairy Tales' (Baba Yaga tales)

name: Firebird's Feather
description: Golden feather of the Firebird (Zhar-ptitsa) of Russian fairy tales, which shines so brightly that it lights a whole dark room and is carried by heroes such as Ivan Tsarevich into the tsar's palace. In Afanasyev's tale the feather, and later the bird itself, is sought as a task set by the tsar; the radiant Firebird became a favourite motif of Russian decorative art.
source: Afanasyev, 'Russian Fairy Tales' ('The Firebird')

name: Vasilisa's Doll
description: Small wooden doll given to Vasilisa by her dying mother in the Russian fairy tale, which eats a morsel of the girl's food and helps her perform impossible tasks so that she survives her cruel stepmother and Baba Yaga. Recorded in Afanasyev's collection as 'Vasilisa the Beautiful', the doll is the helper-object of the tale, a folk counterpart to the magical helpers of later European fairy tales.
source: Afanasyev, 'Russian Fairy Tales' ('Vasilisa the Beautiful')

name: Gusli (Russian Psaltery)
description: Ancient Russian plucked zither, a shallow trapezoid or helmet-shaped board with gut or metal strings, played by the epic singers who performed the byliny. The legendary Novgorod merchant Sadko of the byliny plays the gusli so well that the Sea Tsar summons him to the underwater palace; the instrument is attested in chronicles, miniatures and archaeological finds from Novgorod.
source: Novgorod archaeological finds; byliny of Sadko

name: Samovar (Russian Tea Urn)
description: Metal urn with a central fire-tube used to boil water for tea, a fixture of the Russian home from the early 18th century. The great workshops at Tula and in Moscow produced brass, nickel and silver samovars; around the samovar the family gathered for the evening tea, and it became a byword for hospitality in Russian daily life and literature.
source: Tula State Museum of Samovars; Russian Museum of Decorative Arts

name: Balalaika (Russian Triangular Lute)
description: Three-stringed Russian lute with a characteristic triangular body, plucked or strummed to accompany folk songs and dances. The balalaika became a symbol of Russian folk music in the 19th century, when Vasily Andreyev standardised its sizes into a whole family of instruments; it is played solo and in orchestras, and its bright, percussive tone carries well in open-air music-making.
era: attested from the 17th century; standardised late 19th century
source: Russian folk music tradition; Andreyev's balalaika orchestra (1888)

name: Kokoshnik (Russian Women's Headdress)
description: Crest-shaped ceremonial headdress of Russian women, a stiff crown of brocade, velvet or silk embroidered with pearls, gold thread and beads. Worn over the braids from the 17th century, the kokoshnik varied by region, from horned and high-crested to flat-topped forms, and marked the married woman; after Peter the Great's court reforms it survived as festive wear in the provinces.
material: brocade, velvet, silk, pearls, gold thread
source: Russian Ethnographic Museum; historic Russian dress studies

name: Rushnyk (Ukrainian Ritual Cloth)
description: Embroidered ritual cloth of Ukraine woven from linen or hemp and decorated with geometric and floral embroidery at both ends. The rushnyk hangs on icons, frames doors and windows, joins the couple's hands at weddings and lines the coffin at funerals; its patterns carry protective meaning, and a woman's rushnyk collection testified to her skill.
source: Ivan Honchar Museum; Ukrainian ethnographic collections

name: Pysanka (Ukrainian Decorated Egg)
description: Ukrainian Easter egg decorated by the wax-resist method: a stylus called pysachok draws lines of hot beeswax on the shell, which is then dyed in successive colours, ending with the wax melted away to reveal the pattern. Pysanky bear solar, plant and animal motifs linked to spring rebirth, and eggs were kept in the house as protective charms.
source: Ukrainian pysanka tradition; Lviv Ethnography Museum collections

name: Bandura (Ukrainian Zither-Lute)
description: Plucked string instrument of Ukraine combining a lute's neck with a zither-like soundboard holding up to several dozen strings, played by folk singers called bandurysts and kobzars. The kobzar tradition of singing epic dumy to the bandura is among Ukraine's most distinctive musical heritage; the instrument descends from the older kobza and spread across Ukraine from at least the 18th century.
material: wood body, gut or metal strings
era: attested from at least the 18th century
source: Ukrainian bandura tradition; studies of the dumy epics

name: Polish Pisanki (Decorated Eggs)
description: Polish Easter eggs decorated by several regional techniques: batik wax-resist (pisanki), scratch-carving, and the solid raspberry-dyed eggs called byki. Patterns of rays, stars and plant sprigs vary by region, with Kraków, Łowicz and the Opoczno district known for distinct styles; eggs were exchanged at Easter as gifts and kept in the home as charms.
material: hen's egg, beeswax, dyes, scratching tools
source: National Ethnographic Museum, Warsaw; Polish ethnographic collections

name: Ciupaga (Podhale Axe-Staff)
description: Small axe with a long wooden haft carried by the highlanders (górale) of the Polish Tatra mountains as a walking staff, herding tool and dance prop. The ciupaga's haft is often carved, and highlanders strike it on the floor in the energetic zbójnicki dance; it accompanies the shepherd's life of the Podhale region and is a recognised emblem of Tatra highland culture.
material: steel blade, ash or beech haft
source: Podhale highland culture studies; Tatra Museum, Zakopane
